 A concrete structure could play an important role in protecting future nuclear plants from earthquakes.
 Read Next: ​300–470°F exposure for 10,000 hours degrades aluminum alloy in nuclear fuel casks By Aamir Khollam Energy Nov 18, 2026 10:45 PM EST By Aamir Khollam Nov 18, 2026 10:45 PM EST Rolls-Royce SMR seismic support. Skanska Key Takeaways
 Skanska has successfully built and tested a precast aseismic bearing pedestal for Rolls-Royce SMR at its Bentley Works facility in Doncaster, England.
 The demonstrator validates an off-site manufacturing approach that could improve production quality, consistency and construction schedules.
 Rolls-Royce SMR is testing critical construction methods before deploying them across its planned fleet of factory-built nuclear power plants.
 Rolls-Royce SMR has completed an important construction test for its small modular reactor (SMR) program. A new precast concrete component could help make future nuclear plants easier to manufacture and assemble.
 Skanska built and tested an aseismic bearing pedestal at its Bentley Works facility in Doncaster, England. The demonstrator validates an off-site manufacturing approach for a component that plays a crucial role in protecting nuclear infrastructure during earthquakes.
 The achievement gives Rolls-Royce SMR another construction method to evaluate before deploying its factory-built reactor design. It also demonstrates how conventional construction techniques could support the industrial-scale production of nuclear power plants.
 Testing earthquake protection
 Aseismic bearing pedestals support isolation devices within the Rolls-Royce SMR design. These devices help separate buildings and other structures from ground movement during seismic events.
 The isolation system reduces the forces that earthquakes can transfer into critical infrastructure. Its performance therefore plays an important role in protecting the reactor facility and supporting its structural resilience.
 Skanska’s demonstrator allowed engineers to test the manufacturing approach before committing to full-scale deployment. Producing the component away from the construction site could also give manufacturers greater control over quality and production schedules.

 The prototype represents a first-of-its-kind precast bearing pedestal for the Rolls-Royce SMR design. Skanska completed its construction and technical trials at Bentley Works, bringing its engineering and manufacturing capabilities into the project.
 Factory production takes shape
 Off-site manufacturing forms an important part of the Rolls-Royce SMR construction strategy. The company wants to move significant portions of plant construction into controlled manufacturing environments.
 That approach could reduce the amount of work required at individual construction sites. It could also improve consistency across multiple reactors by allowing suppliers to repeat established manufacturing processes.
 Rolls-Royce SMR Operations and Supply Chain Director Ruth Todd said the demonstrator supports the company’s plans for factory-built nuclear plants. She also pointed to the importance of testing critical components before deployment.
 Early cooperation with suppliers helps engineers identify potential problems before construction begins. It also gives manufacturers time to refine their processes ahead of larger production requirements.
 Skanska UK Executive Vice President Terry Muckian highlighted the engineering work behind the demonstrator. The project combined the contractor’s civil engineering, design and steelwork manufacturing experience.
 UK nuclear plans advance
 Rolls-Royce SMR has secured a place in the UK’s small modular reactor deployment program through Great British Energy – Nuclear. The country’s first planned deployment will take place at Wylfa on Anglesey, North Wales.
 The UK expects the site to generate its first electricity in the mid-2030s. The Czech Republic and Sweden also feature in the company’s international deployment plans.
 Small modular reactors use factory-manufactured sections that engineers assemble at their final locations. This approach aims to make nuclear construction more repeatable than conventional projects.
 The bearing pedestal demonstrator addresses one part of that challenge. Its successful trials give Rolls-Royce SMR and Skanska a tested manufacturing approach for a component that supports seismic protection.
 Further engineering and manufacturing work will determine how the method translates into future plant construction. The broader objective remains consistent production across a fleet of reactors.
